utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the witness, please? So that witness will have the same protective measures as before?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask the usher to give you a piece of paper on which it says your name. Don't say your name but if it is indeed your name, just say yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, a few instructions, like every other witness, I would kindly ask you because of the interpretation into two languages, can you please follow the dot on the monitor in front of you? When the dot stops, then it would be the best time to start giving your answer because the most important thing is that my question and your answer do not overlap. Try to find a medium speed. I know that you don't find yourself in such situations very often but this is really very important. Please bear that in mind and bear in mind another thing. You have protective measures. Do not say anything that would reveal your identity. If there is something like that you wish to say, we will ask to go into private session so that only we in the courtroom can hear what you're say. Let's get down to business. Kindly please introduce yourself to the Court, just briefly, where you were born, what schools you finished and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you organise the defence of Siroki Brijeg? If the answer is yes, how did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes, we were the ones who organised the defence of Siroki Brijeg. First we organised this staff and later on, we started organising units, gradually, because whether we saw that the war was inevitable is it already started in some places in Bosnia-Herzegovina then we started organising units. After the shelling of Siroki Brijeg, I think it was on 6 April, the work intensified so we organised, we established three battalions. The first one was the Poskok Battalion, the second one was the Blatska [phoen] and the third one was the Celinska Bojna Battalion. The staff then decided after the war broke out in Siroki Brijeg, our soldiers who had gone to Croatia to fight in Croatia, they returned to defend their homes and placed themselves at the disposal of the municipal staff. And then the municipal staff made a decision to use these men who had been in the war in Croatia, and to make a special unit composed of those men and this task was given to Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Andabak and they were the ones who established another unit that the municipal staff called Convicts Battalion, because some of its members were those who had been persecuted in the former Yugoslavia, emigrants, and that's how the name was given to this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: All these units participated in the liberation of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No. First they participated in the liberation of Siroki Brijeg and then in the liberation of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And now just briefly, tell me in 1992, did your military engagement stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Actually the engagement of these units --.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And if the answer is yes, how did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes, the engagement was terminated in the late 1992. We had a lot of soldiers, that cost a lot of money, and that's why we demobilised some of the troops except for one unit. That was agreed with the municipal staff in Mostar. They were kept to man the line because the enemy was far enough and could no longer threaten Siroki Brijeg. That's why we carried out demobilisation. We remained, we retained just one unit, the Convicts Battalion was also partly demobilised but by then, they were also decimated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, the demobilised men, did the municipality have any commitment towards them, towards those who were demobilised or those who went and joined wars in some other countries of Europe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: We already had a number of conscripts outside working abroad, so some of them returned and the municipality decided that they could remain abroad but that they had the obligation to pay 300 German marks a month towards the defence of their native town. I would also like to say that we already had about 2.000 conscripts abroad even before the war. They were emigrants working abroad before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you pay salaries to the soldiers of the HVO in Siroki Brijeg? If the answer is yes, how were they paid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: The yes is answer. We didn't call those salaries. The municipal staff made a decision that the money that we received, people didn't work, the war went on for a long time, there was no money, so we decided that money that we received would be given as assistance or aid to the soldiers. We did not call those salaries. And that was carried out through the defence office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sir, I believe that you are the most -- the best person to resolve a dilemma here for the Honourable Court and for myself. First of all, let me ask you who was in charge of the list or the register of conscripts or soldiers who were entitled to salaries? And the second question is going to refer to ranks but first, things first, who was in charge of compiling the list of soldiers who were entitled to salaries?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreter missed that. I think it was the defence department or defence office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, on the English version, I just heard the interpreter say that she had missed something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Perhaps we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe it's too fast, that the interpreters could not follow you, Mr. Krsnik. Would you please repeat your question slowly and one by one? Then ask the witness to answer it one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sir, we have a problem but this is my mistake. I'm more experienced than you. But sometimes I will speed up as well. Let's go back to my first question: Who was in charge of compiling the list, the register of soldiers who were entitled to salaries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: The lists were compiled by the Defence office. My office. My service. And as for the Convicts Battalion, the commander would bring the list to the office, they were volunteers, and they would bring the lists to the office, and we would check those lists. We would take the lists to the municipality and then the commander would come, take over the money, and would distribute the money amongst his soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, it's just two of the Judges have problems with the computer but we will have to manage along until the break. It's just difficult to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now can you tell this Honourable Court whether there were -- what I'm getting at is whether there were any abuses or misuses of these payment lists? Did you come across such things in your office? Were there any attempts to put people on the lists although they did not belong to any of these units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes. There were such things. People were greedy at times, and that's why these lists were double checked by the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the number of soldiers in 1993 in the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: It was a small unit. They had about 50 to 60 soldiers at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did that number go over 60 at any time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No, at no time did it go over 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My second question that we are all interested in, during this hearing, we heard that there were ranks in 1992 or 1993, a colonel, a major, can you please explain to the Honourable Court about ranks in 1993? Were there any ranks, if they did, whether were they introduced and were you personally involved in that process?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: In 1993, there were no ranks. There were just command duties or posts but there were no ranks. The ranks were introduced only later, in 1994. I know that for a fact because every rank assignment has -- had to be notified to the Defence office. They are assigned by the decree of the president. Then this is sent to the unit, and I claim here before you that we never received any such decree on the assignment of any ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Must every rank be published in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So this is newspaper which carries laws and bills?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes. It has to be published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do these official gazettes exist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please, do you know Mr. Mladen Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Since when have you -- do you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: From the beginning of the war, when he returned from emigration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, did Mr. Naletilic play a political or military role during the war in Herzegovina in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No, no. He didn't belong to any party, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did he discharge any duties? Did he have any function in 1993, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes. The municipal assembly, towards the end of 1992, at one of its sessions, removed the entire municipal leadership. The new municipal leadership was appointed, and the -- Mr. Ivan Culjak was appointed mayor. Mr. Naletilic was the deputy mayor but it was a voluntary post and then there was Miro Kraljevic, Zdenko Cosic, Mr. Banozic [phoen] and Marijan Hrkac and myself. I also joined the municipal leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please, can you tell this Honourable Court where was the command of the Convicts Battalion and did soldiers, including the soldiers, members of the Convicts Battalion, where were they stationed, where were -- where were they stationed, the army in Siroki Brijeg, including the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: The command was in Siroki Brijeg and it was one -- it was stationed in one place. All the brigades, all the commands were at one place, and so it was a unique command for everybody and we did not have any barracks. The soldiers mainly stayed at home, and whenever they were needed they would be called and they would be sent out to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please, do you know whether there were any re-establishments or reorganisations throughout 1993? If yes, when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: The answer is yes, yes there were reorganisations, when -- after the demobilisation of some of the troops, the department -- defence office received an order to establish a brigade, and we acted on that order. The brigade was established and then later on it got the name Marijan Hrkac, Cikota, so that's when we established the Siroki Brijeg brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What year are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I'm referring to the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It is too fast. It is impossible for the interpreters to follow you. And witness, I understand that you are eager to give your evidence but you have to understand that whatever you said has to be translated into the other two languages used in this courtroom. So please make a pause after you hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And tell me, after that, were there any re-establishments, realignments, what you told us about, did this happen later in 1993, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: As for these units, they were realigned. In 1993, towards the end of 1993, perhaps the beginning of 1994, we had a re-establishment again. We re-established into a regiment. And then these professional guards brigades were set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did this re-establishment affect the Convicts Battalion? If so, when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: The Convicts Battalion was also re-established. I think it was in mid-1993. It was re-established, because part of the soldiers went to an unit called Kraljevic. It was a special unit that went to Mostar. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the end of 1993. Was there any re-establishment and did this re-establishment affect what you started telling us about now, that is to say the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1993, all these smaller units were disbanded and they all came to be part of the guards brigade and the remainder of the guards brigade was manned by volunteers from all over. That is to say that the Convicts Battalion and all other such groups were extinguished to so to speak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could the witness please speak into the microphone? We have trouble hearing him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, both of you are going so fast in the last ten minutes that I haven't been able to follow. I really, I can hardly take a note. I'm looking at the computer and trying to listen to what you're saying. Could you go back again on -- if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour. Thank you for having cautioned us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: From all the command units were in one place and then the Siroki Brijeg Brigade got the name Marijan Hrkac, Cikota. After that it's really way too fast. And it's important evidence for your client and obviously for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour. Thank you for having cautioned us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, let us move on slowly now. Could you please tell the Honourable Trial Chamber, from 1992, to 1993, the end of 1993, how many re-establishments were there, I'm referring to the units belonging to Siroki Brijeg. Please proceed slowly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1993, we had a re-establishment in Siroki Brijeg set up a brigade which consisted of four companies, battalions, and the same thing happened to the Convicts Battalion, and towards the end of 1993, we had yet another re-establishment. These small units were disbanded, especially the special ones, and all of them became part of the 2nd Guards Brigade a professional unit, and as for the rest of the home guards, according to the order, various regiments were formed in different municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So that Siroki Brijeg Brigade now was re-established towards the end of 1993 and it was transferred to the home guards regiment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not catch the witness's answer it overlapped the question, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, please, wait at least for a few seconds after I finish my question, and then start answering. We really are having a problem now. You mentioned that the brigade changed its name into Marijan Hrkac, Cikota. When did that happen, in which year, do you recall the month as well? And what was the name of the brigade before that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Before that, before that, it was called the Siroki Brijeg Brigade. After one of the great veterans of Siroki Brijeg got killed, Marijan Hrkac, Cikota, the unit was named -- we named it after this hero of ours, this brigade was named the Marijan Hrkac Cikota Brigade. And I think this was in mid-1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please, could you be so kind as to tell the Honourable Trial Chamber from the beginning until the end of 1993, do you personally know who the commander of the Convicts Battalion was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Slow down, please. Just wait a second. Now proceed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: From the beginning of 1993, after the Convicts Battalion was re-established, then Marijan Hrkac Cikota and Ivan Andabak took over the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What about later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Later, that was -- you mean after, after Cikota was killed? Then this was taken over by Zeljko Vukoja, I think his name was. Yes, it was Zeljko Vukoja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: For the transcript, could you please be so kind as to repeat the last name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Vukoja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Fine. Were these the only commanders of the Convicts Battalion or were there others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Those were the only commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, did the Convicts Battalion had some divisions of its own in other towns?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please let us move on to our last topic. Do you know whether there were any detainees in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: It is being claimed here that they were taken out for forced labour. So please tell the Trial Chamber everything you know about this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: They were not taken out for forced labour. That's the way I should put it, because when the military police came -- actually, I'll start from the beginning. A military policeman came to my office and said that there were some detainees at the military police and he asked me whether he could put them up somewhere around there because they would carry out some kind of an interrogation. I said that I didn't know. There are some rooms across the street from my -- across the hall from my office. The left wing was empty because that was where the command of the Siroki Brijeg Battalion was before, so these rooms were empty. There were a few offices there, there was a toilet, there were some beds, and that's the only thing that I said, but then I said that they had to ask the mayor. He asked me, because they were in a hurry, that I call. I telephoned the mayor then, and I said to him, "Mr. Mayor, some people came here from the military police and asked me about detainees. Could we put them up?" And he said, "If it doesn't bother you," I said that this is a separate wing that this couldn't bother me. And then they put them up there. And that's where they were. That's where they stayed. That's also where the mess was. So that is where they got their food every day, and then I carried out mobilisation of four men, four soldiers, they were supposed to guard them. I did that personally at my own initiative, because I also had a cousin who was a prisoner. So I took four men who were serious people, teachers, professors, they were supposed to guard them so that neither the civilians nor the military could come in and mistreat them in any way. Mikulic was there, professor Mikulic. Then Kutle, Lasic, teacher, and I can't remember now the fourth person. He worked at the hotel. At any rate, they were serious men, they live nearby. My messenger went to call them so I mobilised them so that they would guard these prisoners. As for going out to work, I remember when that happened, when the mayor called me. He called me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please slow down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I remember when the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please slow down. We don't have to caution you all the time. Please, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The problem, Mr. Krsnik, is this small courtroom. The witness is looking at you rather than at the monitor. So if we look at -- if you look at the monitor, Witness, and try not to look at Mr. Krsnik, you might slow down. It's just this courtroom is so much smaller than any of the others.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: The mayor called me. The mayor called me, and I went up to see him at the municipality. The director of Novogradnja was there and it's the first time I met him. This is a construction company, Novogradnja. And it was supposed to dig a canal for providing power for radio and TV transmitters. The mayor asked me to mobilise some workers for him because he could not carry it out as he did not have any workers available. I said that I could not carry out this mobilisation at my own initiative because military obligations supersedes work obligation. Then the mayor said, "Well what about those prisoners? Can they?" And I said that they were not under my authority, that they were under the authority of the military police. The mayor then said that he would look into this, that very often these international people came to see him for a cup of coffee, whatever, this institution, and then he would ask whether they could be engaged and the municipality would even pay something because the mayor did not want to smear the name of Siroki Brijeg in any way. After a while, I left and I saw that they did go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know whether that -- they were paid for that work?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I just want to note that the whole issue of use of prisoners for labour or not is not remotely referenced in the witness summary that we've been provided. It's not something I've prepared for in any way in terms of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think at this stage, we have to hear what happened to those prisoners, and I hope that during the breaks, you could prepare your cross-examination. And at the same time, we are very sorry to say, Mr. Krsnik, that if you want to directly examine this witness on certain subjects, you have to inform the other party about the main subjects of your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Stringer was sitting in this courtroom when a witness testified, I don't dare say who, and he exactly described which posts they held, et cetera. And then I heard that testimony and then when the witness came here, then he told me this story and then I said that he could repeat it here. Now, I cannot know everything in advance what each witness knows and what each witness can testify about. Your Honours, please, if this trial is being followed, a witness described everything about this witness and the post of this witness, and the position he held. Mr. Stringer indeed knew everything about this witness. So he can not say things like this to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I could not agree with you that you couldn't know everything about the testimony of this witness because this is a direct examination, not cross-examination. In the cross-examination, that kind of situation might happen but not in direct examination. Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just a brief response, Mr. President. There is no question that witnesses come and you learn things later rather than earlier. I don't doubt that for a second. There is nothing to prevent Mr. Krsnik from simply sending across to us a piece of paper or informing us the day before that in fact it turns out this witness knows about prisoners and labour and we want to ask him about that. And there is nothing to prevent them from just giving us some sort of a notice before time so that we can make some sort of a preparation but it's not anything that we got in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think that request is legitimate. And Mr. Krsnik, you have to take into consideration when we have next witness with the same situation. You may proceed, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour. And also, what my distinguished colleague, Mr. Stringer said, I agree with that, too. Well, any way, we do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We left off at the question whether you personally had any knowledge of this work being paid for to them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: The director came, he brought money, he wanted to give it to me and I said that I was not authorised for this, and I told him to take this to the military police and I told him where the military police was and I honestly don't know anything more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the usher to help us, please. This is the last photograph I have left. This is 26.2. It's an aerial image. Could we please have it placed on the ELMO? Could you please be so kind as to mark where this office of yours was and where these detainees were? And since you'll be doing that any way, could I please ask you to tell me where the command of all these units of Siroki Brijeg was and what happened to the other buildings at the tobacco station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: This is my office, on the left-hand side was this wing, and on the left-hand office was the Defence office, the Defence department and on the other side were those four or five rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please take a magic marker and put a circle around this? And could you please put U.O., meaning "odvjetnik," defence office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now put a circle around that building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: All right. And now, please put a circle -- now please put another circle around the building where the command of all these units at Siroki Brijeg was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, what about these other buildings at this so-called tobacco station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: The others up here, the former hangars, they didn't have any windows or anything. It was also abandoned. There was nothing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, please, could you mark the borders of this tobacco station so Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that we would make things easier perhaps for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: This is perhaps a bit of a trouble, bit of trouble for you, but could you put "A" where your office was and could you put the letter "B" where these offices of the command were, so A and B above those two circles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Are you familiar with the tobacco station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was there any kind of detention centre, prison, or anything like that at the tobacco station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Could you please put this away? I can't follow this, and I don't know when I should give my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Just press button number 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No, no, there was no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Where was the building of the military police, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was in the building of the former committee, that's what we called it, at Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Excuse me, which committee?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Of the Communist Party of the former Yugoslavia. That was across the street from the cinema, and of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions. I think that I've dealt with all the subjects. I forgot something. My colleague reminded me. I would like to put an exhibit before you. P704, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at this, leaf through it? Allegedly, that's what it said here, this is a list for the payment of personal income for November, 1993. And it was written on the 2nd of December, 1993. List for the payment of personal incomes for November, 1993, allegedly all these persons are members of the Convicts Battalion. I would like to lead you because I don't want this to go on too long. Were there any combat groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I can't really call this a document. This is nothing. This has nothing to do with the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: First and foremost, I need to ask you something. It says here Zeljko Radic, Zarko Vedicovic [phoen] and Josip Bosnjak and Jakob Travila [phoen]. That is the command of the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What page are we on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I don't know. In Croatian language, I don't have your number. Third page in Croatian version. [Interpretation] And the number is 00795355.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So did you have a look at it? Was that the command of the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please go to page on which it says SPSN, the Convicts Battalion, 5362 are the last four digits on the page. Tell me, did the Convicts Battalion have the -- have artillery, logistics, mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No. How could a unit consisting of 60 men have all that? We never had any artillery in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And now, SPSN, the Convicts Battalion, have you come to that page? Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Do you know Mr. Ivan Hrkac, who is here under number 7?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Ivan Hrkac, I guess I -- I -- if that is the brother of the late Marijan Hrkac, then yes, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know where he was in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: He was in Croatia, in the Croatian police, I believe, and I think he was in -- on the island of Korcula.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And do you know Mrs. Miranda Lovric, Zana Lovric and Mirjana Barbaric? Were they really members of the Convicts Battalion? They are under numbers 9, 10 and 11.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No. Mirjana Barbaric, I think she was the mother of the late Boka Barbaric, who was killed earlier on. I don't know what she would be doing in the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And now under number 21, Danko Bilinovac. Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: He is the chief of police in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was he a member of the Convicts Battalion in November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No. He was the chief of police at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And then can you go to the next page and look at number 57, 58, 59, 60 and 61? Marijan Hrkac, Mihovil Zdunic, Boro Barbaric, Darko Radman, and Stanislav Kraljevic, do you know these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes, of course I know them. I went to their funerals. They were killed much earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you go to the third page, please? Number 67, Cedo Brkic, 68 Zlatko Spajic, 70, Miljenko Basic, 71, Dragan Ivankovic, 72, Dragan Andric, 73, Mate Markic, 74, Zeljko Velc, 75, Damir Bazina, did you read these names? Did you know these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Not all of them but most of them, yes, I do, and they were also killed, and they were members of the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And can you find the names of any other people who were killed? Do you have any other comments? Look at the back where it says, "Mortars, artillery, signals, logistics." Can you see it where it says 16 people in the logistics? Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Can I comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: If this is a list for salaries, then this is really ridiculous. It's a forgery, nothing else. The Convicts Battalion first of all had only 60 soldiers and according to this list, this looks like a brigade, like a much larger unit, and especially ridiculous and funny, it is where it says that the Convicts Battalion Cico, Cicko, and there was just one Convicts Battalion, the Convicts Battalion of Siroki Brijeg, with 60 men. I really don't know what else to say about this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions. I apologise, I'm sorry. All the time I have been thinking of that and I even have a reminder, a huge reminder so that I don't forget.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, did you ever come across documents where it is typed out that the commander is Mladen Naletilic and the signature is by somebody else, especially by Mr. Ivan Andabak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I suggest there is a better way to address this issue rather than by this leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think so. It's very leading, Mr. Krsnik. You have to pose it another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know how to ask that question. I don't know how to ask my witness whether he has ever come across a document where one name is typed out and the other name is signed. I really don't know how to ask that. And that is exactly what I'm interested in. I really don't know how to go about asking such a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please help me? Whatever you tell me to do, I will do, if you can assist me with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think you question you asked is much better than the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you've heard my questions. Have you ever come across a document where one name is typed out and the signature, handwritten signature is by somebody else? Have you ever come across such documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And now for example, can I now ask, without risking your caution, can you give me an example? Maybe that's the way I should put this question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I'm supposed to give you an example?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes. Have you ever come across such documents where one name is typed out and the signature is by somebody else? Can you give me an example of such a document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes. There were such documents, and especially this was the case with Mr. Andabak. Mr. Andabak would always use that, and I remember there were other people who used that, but to a lesser extent because the command was at the tobacco station where my office was, I even went one time to see him, and I meant to ask him to make sure that the documents that he sent to the defence department be correct, and I meant to ask him to type out his name, and he got a little angry, and he said, "Tuta is our legend, he's the pride of the Convicts Battalion. And for as long as I am its commander, every piece of paper is going to bear his name." And then I left. I did not take the matter any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, are you -- would you prefer to cross-examine this witness for another ten minutes or we break and we come back?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Perhaps in the long run, it would be more efficient to break now so that I can organise myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll break until 10.30. We will have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer? Cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Is it possible I could ask the technical booth to lower the ELMO? My view of the witness is obstructed. That's fine. We are going to use the ELMO in couple of minutes. That's the problem. If there is a way around it. That's satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Douglas Stringer, I'm going to ask you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution. Sir, first let me ask the usher if he could bring four documents that I want to ask you about, 236.01 will be the first. Sir, these documents -- this document, sir, just a quick question. You can take a moment to look at it. I just wanted to ask you whether this appears to be the document which is the document in which you were appointed to the position that you held in Siroki Brijeg, which you testified about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I've looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sir, and perhaps we should go into private session, briefly, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sir, in your capacity in executing the functions of the office that you held in Siroki Brijeg, I believe you testified in your direct that you were involved in the preparation of certificates, membership certificates, the mobilisation, demobilisation, of HVO membership; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Records along those lines, membership certificates, call-up or mobilisation notices, were those records kept in your office in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: The records were sent to the Defence administration after a certain time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: At the time that the records were being made and -- made by you or by your office, were copies of the records kept at the Defence department in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Not all the copies but some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'd ask the witness be shown Exhibit 26.9, which is the photograph. We might want to put it on the ELMO in a few moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, are you able to identify this place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What is this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: This is the perimeter of the tobacco station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In that photograph, are you able to see the place where your office was located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could I ask you to take a maker, the blue marker, and to put a circle around the location of your office? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: On the ELMO, please, just so that we can see where -- what he marked. Okay. Now, Witness, do you know whether -- and I believe you may have marked this already on the other photograph, did the Convicts Battalion have any sort of an office or headquarters in this place we are calling the tobacco station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I've already answered that, the Convicts Battalion and the command of the entire Siroki Brijeg army had its headquarters there, in the tobacco station. Andabak also had an office there within this perimeter, in one of these buildings. I can now see it better. I couldn't see it as well on the previous photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Would you be able to put a circle around the place that was this headquarters for the Convicts Battalion and the other units that you've referred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I should have asked to you put a number 2 just next to that so that we know which place we are referring to in the record.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, you may or may not know, in September of 1998, there was a search and seizure operation which took place in Siroki Brijeg, and investigators of this Tribunal came to Siroki Brijeg and obtained documentation. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes. They were in my office as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: They were in your office that you've circled on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes, in my office. Nothing is marked, where nothing is marked. There is no mark on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: They were in the premises of the tobacco station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we called the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know if they were also present in the place you've marked as number 2, which was the military headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know if the Convicts Battalion accepted foreigners into its ranks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I don't know that, because I only kept records of the conscripts from Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did any members of the Convicts Battalion stay in the Park Hotel during 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: The hotel was open, they may have, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit, sir, is 542.3. It's in the binder. Witness, while he's getting the document, let me ask you this: In terms of mobilising young Croat men to join the HVO, do you recall whether Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, ever personally intervened in your efforts to mobilise members of the HVO? Whether he personally intervened on behalf of any of these young men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Not with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Take a look at this exhibit, sir. This is a photocopy of a document. What you're looking at are the front and back sides of the document, copies of the front and back sides. My question, sir, just looking at the front side or the typed -- the typed side, is this a document that was issued by you or under your direction in respect of the mobilisation of this person named Jozo Cavar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: This first piece of paper, this is a draft notice, but the signature is not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The signature appears over your name, next to a stamp. Are you able to tell us whether in fact this appears to be a mobilisation order that would have been issued by you or on your behalf by someone acting under your authority?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes. This could have been done by one of my clerks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And would a copy of this type of document have been kept in the premises of the Defence office in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: When these are filled out, they are always ready, even in peace time and they are sent either by mail, and we get the receipt, we get a slip, saying that the person has received the mobilisation order, and this is a mobilisation for a soldier, the second part is missing, and the second part -- this is for the soldier. This part is for the soldier and the second part is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What was -- what would have been contained in the second part that's missing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: The same name of the person who has been called, and that that person has received the mobilisation call, on a certain date, at a certain time, and the person's signature, and if this was sent by a messenger, then the messenger would get that, and if it was sent by mail, then the post man would get that slip.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Normally, then, the bottom half, bearing the signature of the recipient, would that have been kept by your offices as a record that the person in fact had received the call-up order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: When the person reports to the office, then we file the name of that person, we open his chart, and then we don't need to keep that part of the call-up paper any longer. So the part testifying that the recipient has received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm a little bit confused. Let's say that someone doesn't want to come join the HVO. Let's say that this gentleman, Mr. Cavar, did not come to the tobacco station as he had been directed to do. If you don't keep, how do you have a record that he had in fact been called and was supposed to have come on a certain day? You don't keep any of the records yourself, how do you have a record that in fact he should present himself to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I already told you, every conscript has its chart and book where his name is recorded, and this is where we record these personal data.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, turning to the next page, which is actually the back side of the document, there is handwritten note over the name Tuta, saying, "Please exempt this person who is already engaged in the Convicts Battalion." Do you recognise this as being a note from Mladen Naletilic, Tuta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No. I am not familiar with Mr. Mladen Naletilic's signature, and secondly, this is not the way how you communicate with a Defence office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 605.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just for the record, I would like to say that the Croatian version differs very much from the English version. In the first sentence it says, "I am kindly asking Mr. Colonel Cavar to except," and so on and so forth, and in the English version it says only, "Colonel Cavar." And this makes a difference, changes the meaning, because Colonel Cavar is no where in the body of the text. It says just, "I'm kindly -- I'm asking Colonel Cavar," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think the interpreters will check this. You may proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, this is another one of these call-up notices issued on the 18th of September, 1993. First question, sir, looking at the form, disregarding the handwriting on it, just the form itself, again, is this the type of call-up notice that would have been issued by your office in the execution of its function?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes. It's the same call-up notice like the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is this one signed by you or is it signed by someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: This isn't my signature either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was it -- did it happen from time to time that others would sign over your -- over your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: If I would be absent, a deputy would be appointed, but this isn't his signature either. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The document itself, though, appears to be -- appears to you to be like many of the others issued by your -- are you able to hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I can barely hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is that a little better now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I can hear the gentleman very nicely but I can't hear the lady who is interpreting. I mean, I can hear her but it's not loud enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's more important for you to hear her than for you to hear me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: That's the problem. I hear you and I don't hear her.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is it improving at all? He's turning up the volume.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: A bit better now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Again just getting back to this form, this appears to be the kind of form issued by your office on a regular basis, calling up individuals to join the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know this person, Ivan Naletilic, whose name is referenced here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, again directing your attention to the handwriting on the upper right-hand corner, this is written note over the name Tuta, indicating that he's not fit. Do you recall any intervention on the part of Tuta on behalf of this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I believe, sir, that another function carried out by your office in Siroki Brijeg related to the preparation of reports of the manpower levels, the strength of the various units located in Siroki Brijeg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No, no. This is probably done by commanders of units. What do I have to do with it? I can only report on the number of persons I had just mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then let me show you the next document, 558.3. Do you know if the Defence office in Siroki Brijeg made reports like this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this report or any reports like this before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I've never seen this report before. You can see up here in the letterhead it hasn't even been filled out. I mean the number is not there. So this document is wrong. I've never seen any such thing. Anybody could have filled this out. The office has its serial number and another number, and all that, and there is none of that here on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll take that answer. Witness, another of the functions that I believe that was executed by your office in Siroki Brijeg later, after the conflict was over, was the granting of disability benefits to HVO members who had been wounded during the course of the conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No. We only made relevant decisions, but we only did that technical aspect of the work involved. We did not set the amounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Let me show you the next group of documents. I think we are talking about the same thing. Starting with 803. Sir, if you just take a moment to look at Exhibit 803, I just simply wanted to ask, is this the sort of decision that you just made reference to in regard to disability of former members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right. This is a decision. This is one that was done by the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just to speed things up, I'm going to ask you to quickly look at the next four exhibits, 804, -- we can just leave them all out. I'm going to -- witness, I'm going to ask you just to look at the next four, and then I'll ask you some questions about them. Is this document, sir, 804, also one of the disability decisions issued by your office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I don't know how I could know that this is 104. There are different numbers up here, so it confuses me a bit. Are we looking at the same documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. The number in the upper right-hand corner ends with the numbers 8365.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes. That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: These are decisions, or rather this is a decision that was drafted by the Defence department. I cannot say whether this was definite, because if it was refused by the commission at the first level or the second level, then I really can't say whether they were legally binding, but what I can say is true, that actually this was drafted by the Defence office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And that's simply what I want to ask you about the next three, 805.1, 807, and 809.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: These two documents, we can reject straight away. We can only keep one of them. You can see for yourself that they haven't been signed or stamped or anything. So I don't see what I can say about them by way of a comment. This one that bears the name of Davor Leto, that one is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: For the record --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: The other ones could have been typed out by anybody. I cannot say a word about this because my signature is not there and there isn't a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. For the record, Mr. President, the Davor Leto decision is Exhibit 805.1. And that's -- the Davor Leto decision is one that you accept, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And also do you accept the decision regarding Fabijan Bosnjak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And do you accept the decision regarding Tomislav Mandic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: For the record that's Exhibit P804.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And sir, just -- you do not accept the decisions regarding Ivica Aleksic and Gordan Kraljevic because they don't bear a stamp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, even though they don't bear a stamp, do these appear to be decisions that were perhaps in an earlier stage of drafting, a document that was made at the defence office but was not -- but is not a final version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No. This can be a first version but I don't know. I mean, I can't accept it this way, there had to be a reason. I mean if they all came from the office, there would be no reason why some would be stamped and others would not be stamped inside. I don't even know these people personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And sir, in drafting these decisions, then, these decisions were based on information about the unit that the person was a member of, and the circumstances under which he became wounded or disabled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Not fully, because -- because when the office drafts, these certificates, that is to say when a person was mobilised, that person is a soldier until demobilised. So there were some units that were not manned by Siroki Brijeg, so there were a lot of transfers, and during the first call-up, we write that down, that a person was mobilised into such and such a unit, but then, when we are released from that unit and transferred to another unit under orders by the Main Staff or whatever, this has to do with these special purposes units, they are not manned by Siroki Brijeg, and of course, military conscripts from Siroki Brijeg can be assigned to these units, then there can be mistakes because I remember when decisions were drafted of this kind we did not have exact insight into the exact units that the person had been to because it wasn't the same, like during the first mobilisation, so sometimes we could have mistakes and I know that I would tell my boss often that we had this problem but he said it was less important. So any way, when we have this written down, which unit this person belonged to, it was less important to us, it was most important that this person was mobilised and that the military medical commission had supplied a document to the military office saying that such and such a person is a disabled person. Then on the basis of the records Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the Defence office, this person would be mobilised and then we would compile these certificates. So we actually took care only of the technical aspect of the exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at just one of these briefly and then we are going to move on. Can I ask you to look at the decision regarding Fabijan Bosnjak? Do you have that one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I hadn't read it in full previously so let me take a look, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about the part that is called "statement of reasons." Because this gives some insight into how these decisions were made. It looks as though there are a number of findings or reasons that are cited as justification for the recommendation on disability. For example, proof that he was born, proof of his date of birth. You see that's the first item. Proof that there are no criminal proceedings against him. Proof that he's not already receiving financial compensation for disability. And all these findings are backed up by certificates or documents. And then again proof that in fact he was the member of the unit, in this case Convicts Battalion, and proof that he was wounded, as indicated here, on the 1st of July, 1993, in Mostar. So in making these decisions, my question was whether your office considered the evidence or the proofs that were supplied then in making a decision whether this person was justified in getting disability.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: These are forms that are used throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They are obtained from the ministry. And this was done by the lawyer in my office. I'm an economist by training. So I could not really draft all the details. I mean I would not really be competent. It's the lawyer who drafted the document, and I would sign it, and I had full confidence in him. So this is really a form. It's a form that is filled out. And as you can see, each and every one of them was filled out appropriately. So this is the way the office did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, I'll ask now we can put all of those away. We are finished with those. I'm going to ask the witness to look again at Exhibit P704, which is the big document. Witness, let me first ask you generally, your testimony was that members of the HVO received what you called assistance or aid. It wasn't called salary. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct, until towards the end of 1993. Then it was only the municipality of Siroki Brijeg that distributed this aid. Other municipalities didn't even do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So at the end of 1993, the Defence department was actually involved in providing aid or some financial compensation to HVO members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: We are not a department. We are an office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry. And in determining who should receive this financial assistance, did the office keep lists of persons who were members of the various units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No. We had files. Every unit had these files, and then they would all be put into a box, and that would constitute the list actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were the lists kept at the tobacco station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: The unit would provide the list, and then we would take out the files, we would look through them, we would circle the names, on the basis of the files, on the basis of what we had in the files. And then that would be taken back and then payments would be issued on that basis. People would sign for them. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But you mentioned a box with all the files in it. Was that box kept in the tobacco station? Either in the military headquarters that was located in one part or in the Defence office that was located in a different part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Well, I didn't mention any binders. I said files. I wish I had one of those files here with me so I could show it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. May I have just a moment, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we might have a document in the courtroom that is what is being described by the witness. We -- Mr. Scott has got it as part of his preparation for another witness. So we've only got one copy but with the Court's permission I would like to show it to the witness. We could put it on the ELMO, and simply see what he has to say about it, if it's agreeable to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see there is no difficulties for doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This has already been marked as Exhibit P938. Perhaps the usher can let the Defence take a quick look at it first and then we will show it to the witness. If it's agreeable I could go ahead on to another subject and we could come back to this if the Defence wants a little more time. Okay. If the usher would show this to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence has no objections, especially if the witness can actually explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you could give the witness the Croatian language version and put the English version on the ELMO or the first page of the English version so that the Trial Chamber can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, I simply don't know whether this is the kind of document that you were just describing, whether you can give us any information about what you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No, no. This file is actually a single card, name and surname of the soldier, year of birth, did his military service where, when, mobilised into such and such a unit, took part in the war from such a date to such a date. It's a completely different type of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Just on this document now, 938, is this a different kind of document that was kept in the tobacco station, to your knowledge, either at the military headquarters or in the defence office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: We never had such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll withdraw the exhibit, Mr. President. I don't think the witness knows anything about it. The next exhibit is 506. This is not on the list previously distributed. It's something that we pulled during the break. We can put the English version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked --?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We have copies to distribute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, while that's being distributed, I can just ask you a few questions about it. You were asked in a way about the signing of names by one person over the name of another person. You talked about Mr. Andabak. Would you agree with me, sir, that Mr. Andabak signed literally hundreds of document, perhaps in the same format that appears on this particular document? That is signing his name over the typed name of Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, who is indicated as the commander of the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that. I cannot guarantee that this is Mr. Ivan Andabak's signature. I don't know how I can accept this claim. I never paid too much attention to the way he signed his name on documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that throughout 1993 and 1994, and even later, many, many documents were written, drafted, which identify the commander of the Convicts Battalion, independent special purposes unit, as Mladen Naletilic, Tuta? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I only know that Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, was the commander of the Convicts Battalion up to 1992. That is what it says in my records, in the defence office, that's how his name is filed in our records. And after that, a new commanders replaced him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about Mr. Naletilic for a few moments. He was widely regarded as having been a key figure in the liberation first of Siroki Brijeg and then of Mostar in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: He was widely respected throughout Western Herzegovina as a key military figure in respect of the conflict with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No. He was not a key military figure. He was the commander of the Convicts Battalion, the unit from Siroki Brijeg, which participated in the liberation of Siroki Brijeg and Mostar. He didn't have a key military, overall military role.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, in your -- based on your knowledge, sir, what was his role in respect of the Convicts Battalion, if it was not a military one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Which period do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: 1992. When I said that he did not have a key role overall role for the liberation of Mostar because there were a number of units which participated in that effort. He was the commander of the Convicts Battalion. But the liberation of Mostar involved other units, units from Mostar, Citluk and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And your testimony that he was not the commander of the Convicts Battalion in 1993, is that based on the fact, as you say, that you didn't have a written document confirming that he was the commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No, because we were together in the municipal leadership. I told you that. He did not wear a uniform in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: He did not wear a uniform in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: He would not come to the municipality building wearing a uniform. He may have been wearing it at times but I know for a fact that he was not the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, that he was in Mostar at the HVO Defence Ministry on the 10th of May, 1993? At the time the conflict with the an Armija was taking place? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you know that he was in Doljani in the Jablanica municipality on the 19th of April, 1993, when Boka Barbaric was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not out on the ground. I was the chief of Defence office. So I -- there is no way for me to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You testified, sir, about -- you told a story about some detainees who had come to Siroki Brijeg, and there had been some discussion about whether to pay them. Just a few questions about that. What is the time frame? Can you tell us what month and year you were talking about when this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I think -- it was in 1993, I think it was mid-1993, in June, I should think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: As a point of reference, there was a conflict between the HVO and the Armija in Mostar on the 9th of May, and then there was another important conflict that occurred on the 30th of June, 1993, when the Armija attacked the HVO Northern Camp. Are you able to tell us this incident involving the prisoners in Siroki Brijeg, was it before the 9th of May, after the 9th of May, before the 30th of June, are you able to give us an idea?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I can't. They were brought by the military police. I really don't know where they were taken prisoner. I can't -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Because I thought you testified that one was a professor or that they held some sort of position that sounded civilian to me. Was I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes, you have misunderstood me. I told you that these people, these professors and teachers, were guarding these prisoners. I wasn't referring to the prisoners when I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Where did they work, those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know -- can you give us any greater detail about the location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: The machinery, as far as I could see, the machines were digging where they could, where the machinery couldn't go, they would go. Through Siroki Brijeg, up towards a little hill above Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is that called Gypsy Hill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: No. It's not the Gypsy Hill, not Cigansko Brdo. This is towards the left. And where they were digging is more towards the right, eastwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were Muslim prisoners held at the MUP station in Siroki Brijeg? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't believe it. The MUP is a civilian institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know if the mufti of Mostar, Kasim Mezit, was held in the MUP station, on approximately the 8th, 9th, 10th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: I never heard of such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Exhibit P171. I'll be able to finish before the break. I assume we are breaking at quarter to, Mr. President? Or is that -- 171.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before we talk about that, let me ask you, Witness, in the town of Siroki Brijeg, perhaps the municipality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I'm sorry, my learned friend, can we also have this exhibit? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have an extra copy? Any way, we'll put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's the Narodni List. It's something we pulled at the break, Mr. President. We can put it on the ELMO. We can show these passages to counsel. It's the gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to direct you on the bottom of the page ending 6645. So the usher can find that for you. And while he's doing that, I'll ask you a different question. Throughout the town of Siroki Brijeg, for a long time after the conflict, maybe even today, have you seen posters around Siroki Brijeg of Mr. Naletilic wearing a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: There were posters. I've seen them. But that was some three years ago. But I can't remember whether he was actually wearing a camouflage uniform on these posters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to direct you now to this page 6645. You testified about ranks or the lack of ranks in the HVO, you said that they had to be published in the Official Gazette. Now, you've been shown a part of the Narodni List, Official Gazette publication, and I'm asking you to first look at this decision on salaries and remuneration for members of the armed forces. I'll go very slowly because I know the interpreters don't have this. Going --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Excuse me, since we don't have a copy, could we have a date on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, this is the September, 1992 issue of the Narodni List.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And witness, I'm going to direct you particularly to Article number 6, which is on the next page of the English version. The bottom of the first page. It appears to me, sir, that in this decision, there is a reference to different grades or ranks within the HVO that would then determine the amount of compensation, soldier, squad commander, platoon commander, company commander, do you see all those? Moving on to the next page of the English, battalion commander, brigade commander, operative group commander.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NQ
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that but these are not ranks. These are command posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
